pedagogy.summary: For 5–7s this introduces the skeleton as the hard framework INSIDE the body doing three jobs: giving the body its shape and holding it up (support), protecting soft important organs (the skull is a helmet for the brain, the ribcage a cage for the heart and lungs), and — with muscles — letting the body move. The key, often-missed idea for this age is that MUSCLES PULL on bones to move them; muscles don't push. Teach it on the child's own body: feel the hard skull, the ribs, the spine down the back; feel a muscle (the upper arm) bunch up when it works. Name just a few bones/groups (skull, ribcage, spine, leg bones) and keep muscle action to 'muscles pull bones' — the paired push/pull detail comes later. Correct the common ideas that bones are dead sticks or that we're 'like jelly' inside; the skeleton is a living, supportive, protective frame.
bestPractices: Use the child's own body as the manipulative: feel the hard skull, ribs and spine, and feel an arm muscle bunch when it lifts — so structure and function are felt, not just seen.
Teach the three jobs with vivid protection images (skull = helmet for the brain, ribcage = cage around the heart and lungs) — the most memorable hook at this age.
Establish early that MUSCLES PULL bones to move them (they can't push), setting up the antagonistic-pair idea later without over-complicating now.
Name only a few bones/groups (skull, ribcage, spine, leg bones) and locate them on the body, keeping the load age-appropriate.
Confront 'bones are dead/just sticks' and 'we're squishy with no frame' — the skeleton is a living frame that supports and shapes us.
keyRepresentations: A simple labelled skeleton showing shape/support (the frame that holds us up)
Protection images: skull-as-helmet over the brain, ribcage-as-cage around heart/lungs
The child's own body — feeling hard bones (skull, ribs, spine) and a working muscle
Muscle-pulls-bone shown as a muscle shortening to move a limb
A 'no skeleton' contrast (a floppy body) to show why we need a frame
commonMisconceptions: 'Bones are dead / just hard sticks' — they are living parts that grow and even make blood.
'Muscles push bones to move them' — muscles PULL (shorten) to move bones; they can't push.
'The skeleton is only in the arms and legs' — missing the skull, spine and ribcage.
'Without a skeleton we'd still stand up' — missing that the frame gives shape and support (we'd be floppy).
'The skull is solid all the way through' — it's a protective case around the brain.
'Bones and muscles are the same thing' — bones are the hard frame; muscles are the soft parts that pull them.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, introduce the skeleton as the hard, living framework inside the body that does three jobs: giving the body shape and holding it up (support), protecting soft important organs (skull as a helmet for the brain, ribcage as a cage for the heart and lungs), and — working with muscles — letting the body move. The often-missed key idea for this age is that muscles PULL on bones to move them; they do not push. Teach it on the child's own body: feel the hard skull, ribs and spine, and feel an upper-arm muscle bunch up when it lifts. Name only a few bones/groups (skull, ribcage, spine, leg bones). Confront the common ideas that bones are dead sticks or that we are squishy with no frame.

activities.title: Tap-to-explore skeleton: name the bones and reveal their jobs
feedback: If the child names only arm/leg bones, point them to tap the skull, spine and ribcage too so the whole frame is covered.
When a flap is opened, confirm the pairing: skull→brain, ribcage→heart and lungs.
If the child says bones are dead, reveal the living-bone flap and note that bones grow and make new blood cells inside them.
activities.rationale: Naming a few bones and the protection idea is the age-appropriate core; tap-to-reveal with protection flaps mirrors a child exploring their own body and makes structure–function concrete. Optional flaps and highlights are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Pupils should identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement (statutory at Year 3; this KS1 version is a foundational precursor).
The skeleton provides support and shape, protects internal organs (skull–brain, ribcage–heart/lungs), and works with muscles for movement; muscles produce movement by contracting (pulling) on bones.
learnerActions: Look at a simple labelled child-figure skeleton and tap the skull, ribcage, spine and leg bones one at a time; each part highlights and names itself.
Open a 'what does this protect?' flap on the skull to find it is a helmet around the brain, and on the ribcage to see it caging the heart and lungs.
Open a lift-the-flap on a bone to discover bones are alive, grow, and even make new blood cells inside them, busting 'bones are dead sticks'.
For each part, say out loud its job: 'the skull protects my brain', 'the leg bones hold me up'.
activities.intendedInsight: The hard frame inside you gives your body shape and guards the soft, important parts inside; bones are living, not dead sticks.

activities.title: Feel your own frame
feedback: If the child can't locate the spine, guide their hand down the centre of the back to feel the bumpy line.
Confirm each match: 'Yes — that hard part is your ribcage, caging your heart and lungs.'
activities.rationale: Using the child's own body as the manipulative lets structure and function be felt, not just seen, which is a strong, memorable hook at this age; pictures and flaps show structure–function but do not by themselves elicit this physical sensation.
learnerActions: Press the top and back of your head to feel the hard skull; run your fingers down the middle of your back to feel the spine; press the front of your chest to feel the ribs.
Match each hard part you feel to the same part on the picture.
Say which soft organ each hard part is guarding (skull→brain, ribs→heart and lungs).
activities.intendedInsight: The bones you can feel on your own body are the same frame shown in the picture, and they shield the soft parts inside.

activities.title: Make it move / take the skeleton away
feedback: If the child says the muscle pushes, replay the shortening and have them feel the pull in their own arm: muscles only pull.
If the child says the arm bends by itself, point out that to bend your arm yourself, a muscle must pull the bone.
When the figure flops after removing the skeleton, link it back: the frame gives shape and holds us up.
activities.rationale: A live 'make it move / take away the skeleton' interaction can show the muscle-pulls-bone and support ideas vividly; keep the detail of paired muscles pulling in opposite directions (antagonistic pairs) for later and keep the rig toy-simple for this age. The toggle and live muscle-shortening are illustrative examples of the mechanism, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: The skeleton provides support and shape, protects internal organs (skull–brain, ribcage–heart/lungs), and works with muscles for movement; muscles produce movement by contracting (pulling) on bones.
Pupils should identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement (statutory at Year 3; this KS1 version is a foundational precursor).
learnerActions: On a simple toy-like rig, tap a muscle on the figure's arm and watch it shorten and pull the limb so the arm bends.
Squeeze your own upper arm while you bend your elbow and feel the muscle get hard and pull.
Flip a 'remove skeleton' toggle and watch the figure flop, then say why a frame is needed to stand up.
Say in your own words: 'muscles pull on bones to move them.'
activities.intendedInsight: Muscles pull (shorten) on bones to move them — they don't push — and without the skeleton the body would flop with no shape or support.

activities.title: Boneless-animal reasoning check
feedback: A full answer explains support/protection (naming an organ shielded) AND that muscles pull on bones to move them, using the boneless animal to justify why we need a frame.
If the child gives only one half (shape/protection OR movement), ask the missing part directly.
If the child says muscles push, re-establish that muscles only pull (tighten and shorten).
activities.rationale: Asking a child to reason about a boneless animal and to explain what moves the arm surfaces both the support/protection role and the muscle-pulls-bone idea. This can be used during teaching as well as for checking; recognition-only matching does not itself elicit the child's own spoken explanation.
sourceClaims: Pupils should identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement (statutory at Year 3; this KS1 version is a foundational precursor).
learnerActions: Think about a jellyfish, which has no bones at all.

Say what a jellyfish can't do that you can because you have a skeleton (for example, stand up tall on land or keep its shape out of water) — remembering that a jellyfish can still swim using its muscles.
Answer the two-part question: why do you have a hard skeleton inside you, and when you bend your arm to lift a cup, what makes the arm actually move?
activities.intendedInsight: The skeleton is needed for firm shape, support and protection of soft organs, and movement comes from muscles pulling on bones.

activities.title: Optional: match and quick-check
feedback: If the match is wrong, return to the labelled figure or the child's own body to re-feel and re-name the part.
If 'push' is chosen, re-establish that muscles only pull.
activities.rationale: A short matching/labelling activity checks recall of bone names and protection pairings. Recognition-only tasks confirm recall but do not by themselves elicit the child's own explanation, so use them after the exploratory work.
learnerActions: Match each bone to the organ it protects (skull→brain, ribcage→heart and lungs).
Answer the quick question: do muscles push or pull to move bones?
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate bone names, what each protects, and that muscles pull.

constraints: Keep muscle action to 'muscles pull bones'; the detail that muscles work in pairs that pull in opposite directions (antagonistic pairs) comes later and should not be introduced now.
Name only a few bones/groups (skull, ribcage, spine, leg bones) to keep the cognitive load age-appropriate for 5–7.

A labelled picture, flaps and toggles are scaffolds and illustrative interactions that show structure–function; they do not by themselves elicit the physical sensation of feeling one's own hard bones and working muscle. Feeling one's own body is a recommended hook at this age, not a universal requirement for learning.
A matching/labelling quiz confirms recall of names and pairings but does not on its own elicit the child's own explanation; use alongside, not instead of, exploratory and explanatory tasks.
An optional 3D spin can aid orientation but is not required for naming and protection at this age; naming and protection can also be conveyed in 2D.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row asserted that 3D 'adds nothing' and that a quiz 'assesses rather than builds understanding' as near-absolutes; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, since catalog fit ratings do not establish universal pedagogical necessity.
One listed source (Encyclopaedia Britannica) is marked verified:false in the row; its claim is retained but should be independently confirmed before relying on it as evidence.

The push-vs-pull correction is biologically sound for this age: muscles generate force by contracting (pulling); movement in the opposite direction is produced by a different muscle, which is deliberately deferred here.

activities[1] ('Feel your own frame') has sourceClaims set to [] because its rationale concerns the manipulative method's memorability, which no cited claim supports; the protection facts it practises are source-cited in activities 0 and 2.

Two original misconceptions — 'the skull is solid all the way through' and 'bones and muscles are the same thing' — are addressed only implicitly (skull as a case around the brain; distinguishing the hard frame from soft pulling muscle). Add a dedicated prompt if explicit coverage is wanted.

probeDeeper: Squeeze your upper arm while you bend your elbow — can you feel a muscle getting hard and pulling? What is it pulling on?
Which bone protects your brain, and which bones protect your heart and lungs?
A jellyfish has no bones at all. What can't a jellyfish do that you can, because you have a skeleton?
assess.correctAnswer: Without a skeleton the body would have no firm shape or support — it would flop and couldn't stand up, and the soft organs inside (like the brain and heart) would have no hard casing to protect them. The arm moves because muscles attached to the bones pull on them: when a muscle tightens it pulls the bone and bends the arm. Bones can't move themselves — muscles move them.

errorPatterns.pattern: The skeleton isn't important — bones don't do much and the body would be fine without them.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the jobs concrete: bones give shape and hold you upright, and hard bones shield soft organs; picture a body with no frame.
errorPatterns.distractor: Nothing much — you'd still stand and move the same without bones.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't state a job for the skeleton; thinks the body would work the same without it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Muscles make bones move by pushing them.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that muscles can only PULL (they tighten and shorten); feel the arm muscle pull the bone.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the muscle pushes the bone to move it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bones move on their own — the arm just bends by itself with no muscle.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Connect movement to muscles pulling bones; nothing moves without a muscle acting on it.
errorPatterns.distractor: The arm bends by itself — nothing has to pull it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the arm bending with no mention of muscles.

responseLevels.gap: Can't say what the skeleton is for, or thinks the body would move the same without it; no muscle-pulls-bone idea.
responseLevels.full: Explains the skeleton supports and protects (naming an organ it shields) AND that muscles pull on bones to move them — reasoning about a boneless animal to justify support.
responseLevels.partial: Knows bones give shape/protection OR that muscles move the body, but not both, or thinks muscles push rather than pull.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Why do you have a hard skeleton inside you — what would happen to your body without it? And when you bend your arm to lift a cup, what makes the arm actually move?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who can't say what bones are for, or who thinks the arm bends by itself or that muscles push, reveals the gap. Only a child linking skeleton to support/protection AND muscle-pulls-bone answers both. The tier-two 'what makes the arm move' forces the muscle role to surface.
